title: I Am the LORD: The Promise Restated and a Priestly Family
summary: God answers Moses' complaint by restating his name, his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and a string of promises: he will bring Israel out, redeem them, take them as his people, and bring them into the land. The Israelites, crushed by their labor, do not listen, and Moses again protests that he cannot speak. A genealogy of Reuben, Simeon, and especially Levi then places Moses and Aaron in Israel's family tree before the story resumes.
story: Chapter 5 ended with Moses asking why God had made things worse. God does not explain the delay. He tells Moses who he is and what he will do, and the promise in verses 6 to 8 is a summary of the rest of the Pentateuch and the book of Joshua: rescue from Egypt, a covenant that makes Israel God's people, and entry into the land sworn to the patriarchs. For the first time in Exodus, though, a word from God does not produce faith. The people who believed in 4:31 are now too broken to listen (verse 9). The narrative then pauses for a genealogy that establishes who Moses and Aaron are, and verses 28 to 30 pick up exactly where verse 12 left off. Chapter 7 begins the confrontation that the whole introduction has been building toward.
historical:
The genealogy in verses 14 to 25 begins as if it were going to list all twelve sons of Jacob, with Reuben and Simeon given exactly the sons Genesis 46 assigns them, but it stops at Levi, the third son, because Levi is the point. It lists the three Levite clans (Gershon, Kohath, and Merari), traces Kohath's line to Amram and to Aaron and Moses, and then follows Aaron's line through Eleazar to Phinehas. Later readers would recognize many of the names. Nadab and Abihu died for offering unauthorized fire (Leviticus 10:1-2), and Mishael and Elzaphan, named here as sons of Uzziel, carried their bodies out (Leviticus 10:4). Korah led a rebellion against Moses (Numbers 16), though his line survived (Numbers 26:11) and his descendants appear in the headings of several psalms. Eleazar succeeded Aaron as high priest, and Phinehas became known for his zeal (Numbers 25). The list functions as a priestly record, showing the credentials of the men who will speak to Pharaoh and of the family that will serve at the tabernacle.

The list raises a chronological question. Kohath went down to Egypt with Jacob (Genesis 46:11), and the lifespans given for Kohath (133 years) and Amram (137 years), together with Moses' age of eighty at the exodus, cannot fill the 430 years of Exodus 12:40 if each link is parent to child. Many interpreters think the genealogy names clan heads and skips generations, as biblical genealogies often do. Others connect its four generations from Levi to Moses with the promise that Abraham's descendants would return in the fourth generation (Genesis 15:16) and read the 430 years in the way the ancient Greek translation does, counting the patriarchs' time in Canaan as well (see chapter 12).
cultural:
In the ancient world a name was more than a label. To give someone your name was to reveal something of your character and to make yourself available to be called on. The patriarchs knew God as El Shaddai, God Almighty (Genesis 17:1), the God who promised them children and land. Now the promised things are about to happen, and God says Israel will know him by the name that belongs to keeping those promises.

The last verb of the three in verse 6 comes from Israel's family law. The redeemer, the go'el, was the nearest male relative, responsible to buy back a kinsman who had sold himself into slavery (Leviticus 25:47-49) or to recover family land that had been sold (Leviticus 25:25). When God says “I will redeem you,” he is taking the role of Israel's next of kin. The outstretched arm answers Egyptian royal imagery. From the earliest dynasties, Egyptian art shows Pharaoh with arm raised to strike down his enemies, and royal inscriptions praise the king's mighty arm. Here the arm that saves belongs to the LORD, and it will be raised against Pharaoh. Jewish tradition from the rabbinic period later tied the four cups of wine at the Passover meal to the promises of verses 6 and 7: I will bring you out, I will deliver you, I will redeem you, I will take you. Amram's marriage to his father's sister (verse 20) is recorded without comment, although the law given at Sinai later forbids it (Leviticus 18:12).
literary: Verses 2 to 8 are framed by the words “I am the LORD,” which open the speech, stand at the head of the promises in verse 6, and close it in verse 8. Between them comes a string of first-person verbs: I appeared, I established, I have heard, I have remembered, I will bring out, deliver, redeem, take, bring in, and give. God is the actor in every sentence, and Israel receives. The narrative after the speech uses a technique called resumptive repetition. Moses' objection that he is “unskilled in speech” appears in verse 12, the genealogy interrupts, and the same objection returns in verse 30, so the reader knows the story has picked up where it paused. Verses 26 and 27 point the genealogy's moral: “It was this Aaron and Moses” to whom the LORD spoke, and they are the ones who spoke to Pharaoh. Aaron is named first in verse 26, by birth order, and Moses first in verse 27, by role.

outline.t: God restates his name and his promises
The people cannot listen, and Moses objects again
The heads of the families of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi
This Aaron and Moses: the story resumes

doctrines.note: God's answer to Moses' crisis is a fresh revelation of himself, opening and closing with “I am the LORD.” His name carries his faithfulness: he is the God who hears, remembers, and acts on what he has sworn.

The rescue happens because God remembers the covenant he made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (verses 4 and 5). Verse 7 states the heart of every biblical covenant: “I will take you as My own people, and I will be your God.”

Verse 6 gives the Old Testament's basic vocabulary of salvation: bringing out, delivering, and redeeming. Salvation here is God's own act on behalf of people who can do nothing, and it comes before the law, not as a reward for keeping it.

words.note: YHWH, the personal name of the God of Israel, written with four Hebrew consonants and probably pronounced something like Yahweh. It is connected with the verb to be, as God's self-description in 3:14 suggests. Out of reverence Jewish readers came to avoid pronouncing it and said Adonai, Lord, in its place; most English Bibles follow that custom by printing LORD in small capitals. The form Jehovah arose later from combining the consonants of the name with the vowels of Adonai.

Shaddai, usually translated Almighty, in the phrase El Shaddai, God Almighty (verse 3). Its original meaning is uncertain. Proposals connect it with mountains, with a word for the breast (suggesting the God who nourishes and makes fruitful), or with sufficiency; the familiar rendering Almighty goes back to ancient translations. In Genesis the name appears with promises of children and blessing (Genesis 17:1; 28:3; 35:11).

Ga'al, to redeem, to act as next of kin. The go'el bought back an enslaved relative or family land and could avenge a murdered kinsman. It is the word behind Boaz in the book of Ruth and behind the title Redeemer in Isaiah. Its first use for God's act toward Israel is here in verse 6, and it frames the exodus as family business: God is reclaiming his own.

Arel, uncircumcised. Moses literally calls himself uncircumcised of lips in verses 12 and 30, which the BSB renders as unskilled in speech. The image suggests lips that are closed off or unfit for their purpose, and it echoes the circumcision scene of 4:24-26. Jeremiah later uses the same word of ears that cannot hear (Jeremiah 6:10).

christ: The New Testament takes up the language of this chapter to describe what Christ has done. Paul writes that God sent his Son “to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons” (Galatians 4:5), and Titus speaks of Christ giving himself “to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession” (Titus 2:14), echoing God's promise to take Israel as his own people. The covenant formula of verse 7 runs through the prophets, where Jeremiah promises a new covenant with the words “I will be their God, and they will be My people” (Jeremiah 31:33), and it reaches its end in Revelation, where God dwells with his people and “They will be His people” (Revelation 21:3). Even the genealogy touches the Gospel story. Aaron's wife Elisheba is the sister of Nahshon, whom Matthew lists among the ancestors of Jesus (Matthew 1:4), and her name in its Greek form is Elizabeth, the name of John the Baptist's mother, who Luke says was a daughter of Aaron (Luke 1:5). Those links are family history rather than prophecy, but they show the priestly and royal lines of Israel converging on the one Hebrews calls a priest greater than Aaron.

hard.q: God says he did not make himself known to the patriarchs by the name the LORD, yet Genesis uses the name often. How do these fit?
hard.a:
In Genesis the name appears in the narrator's voice from chapter 2 on, people call on it as early as Genesis 4:26, and God speaks it himself to Abraham, “I am the LORD, who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans” (Genesis 15:7), and to Jacob (Genesis 28:13). Yet verse 3 says, “by My name the LORD I did not make Myself known to them.”

Three main answers are given. Many critical scholars see here evidence of different sources: one tradition, usually identified as the priestly source, held that the name was first revealed to Moses, while another assumed it was known from the beginning, and the final editor let both stand. Many traditional interpreters, Jewish and Christian, argue that to know God's name in the Bible means to know his character by experience, not merely the sound of a word. The patriarchs used the name but lived by promises they never saw kept; Israel is about to learn what the name means as God redeems them. On this reading the verse contrasts two stages of knowing, not ignorance and knowledge of a word. A third, smaller group notes that the narrator of Genesis, writing after Sinai, may use the name for the God the patriarchs worshiped even where they would have said El Shaddai, and some read the second half of verse 3 as a rhetorical question expecting the answer yes. Each view takes the text seriously; they differ on how the Pentateuch came together and on what knowing a name means.

questions: God answers Moses' why not with an explanation but with a renewed statement of who he is. When has knowing God's character carried you further than an explanation would have?
The Israelites could not listen “on account of their broken spirit and cruel bondage” (verse 9). How should that shape the way we speak about God to people who are exhausted or crushed?
The genealogy includes names like Korah, Nadab, and Abihu, who later failed badly. What does it mean to you that God works through real families with mixed histories?
